explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Paul, the apostle writing to the church in Corinth, says it plainly: "each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband." He gives his reason right in the verse: there is so much sexual immorality. Notice he says "his own" and "her own." One spouse each, no sharing, no swapping.

explanations.answer: An elder to watch over them
explanations.explanation: I get the thinking, friend. An elder with a clipboard sounds very official. But Paul doesn't mention an elder anywhere in this verse. He says each man should have his own wife and each woman her own husband, because there is so much sexual immorality.

Ha, that one would make for a hungry week, friend. But Paul doesn't set up any fasting day in this verse. What he says is that "each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband." Prayer does come up a few verses later, but that's a different card.

Close, friend, but the verse runs both ways. Paul says, "The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband." See that "likewise"? It's doing the heavy lifting. The duty belongs to both of them, not just the husband.

You caught the "only," baker. Paul says, "The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband." That little word "likewise" puts the duty on both of them. Nobody gets to sit this one out.

Right on, baker. Paul says, "The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife." It goes both directions, word for word. Nobody in that marriage is holding all the authority by themselves.

I can see why it might sound lopsided, friend, but read it again. Paul says the wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Then he adds, "Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife." So it's true both ways, and the "likewise" is the proof.

explanations.answer: By mutual consent for a time of prayer
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says, "Do not deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time, so you may devote yourselves to prayer." Count the conditions: both agree, it lasts only for a time, and it's for prayer. That's a pretty tight recipe.

explanations.answer: When one of them is away on a journey
explanations.explanation: Travel does make for some lonely evenings, friend. But Paul doesn't list a journey as the exception. The text gives one: "by mutual consent and for a time, so you may devote yourselves to prayer." Both spouses agree, and it's for prayer.

explanations.answer: During the days of a feast
explanations.explanation: A feast sounds like a good time for a break, friend, but Paul never says that here. He says, "Do not deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time, so you may devote yourselves to prayer." No feast days are mentioned. Just agreement and prayer.

That's the one, baker. Paul says to come together again, "so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control." So the pause is for a time, and then they return to each other. The text names Satan as the one doing the tempting.

The world has plenty of tempting going on, friend, I won't argue. But Paul names someone specific here. He says to come together again "so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control."

Nosy neighbors, huh? I get it, they can be a lot. But Paul doesn't blame the neighbors in this verse. He says to come together again "so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control."

Almost, friend, but Paul says the opposite. Right after that verse about prayer, he says, "I say this as a concession, not as a command." So he's telling them plainly that this part is not an order. It's a concession.
You've got it, baker. Paul says, "I say this as a concession, not as a command." So he's not handing down an order here. He's saying clearly what kind of statement it is.

Yes, baker. Paul says, "each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that." He wishes all men were as he is, but he doesn't turn that wish into a rule. Different people, different gifts.

Whoa, friend, that's a heavy word. Paul doesn't call it a burden. He says, "each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that." From God, and a gift.

explanations.answer: To remain unmarried as he is
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Paul says, "It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am." He's speaking to the unmarried and widows here. And he says "as I am," so he's pointing to his own situation.

explanations.answer: To marry as soon as they can
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. For the unmarried and widows, Paul says, "It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am." He does talk about marrying in the very next verse, but that's for people who cannot control themselves. It's not an "as soon as you can" kind of thing.

explanations.answer: To move back with their families
explanations.explanation: Moving home isn't something Paul brings up, friend. To the unmarried and widows he says, "It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am." Nothing in these verses mentions where they should live.

Close, friend, but Paul gives them another way. He says, "But if they cannot control themselves, let them marry." Then he adds, "For it is better to marry than to burn with passion." So the one who can't control himself isn't told to stay single.

That's it, baker. Paul says, "But if they cannot control themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion." Staying unmarried was what he called good in the verse before. This verse is for the ones who cannot control themselves.

explanations.answer: She must not separate from her husband
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Paul says, "To the married I give this command (not I, but the Lord): A wife must not separate from her husband." He marks it as the Lord's command, not his own. That label matters.

explanations.answer: She must pray for her husband daily
explanations.explanation: Praying for a husband is a lovely thing, friend, but it isn't what this command says. Paul writes, "A wife must not separate from her husband." He calls it a command from the Lord, not from himself.

explanations.answer: She must keep her husband's customs
explanations.explanation: Customs aren't in this verse, friend. Paul's command, which he says is from the Lord and not from him, is this: "A wife must not separate from her husband." That's the whole command.

explanations.answer: Stay unmarried or be reconciled to him
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Paul says, "But if she does, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband." Two options, and he lays them out right there. Reconciled means coming back together with him.

explanations.answer: Remarry or go back to her family
explanations.explanation: Not those two, friend. If a wife does separate, Paul says, "she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband." Remarrying isn't one of her options in this verse, and going back to her family isn't mentioned at all.

explanations.answer: Wait a year or ask the elders
explanations.explanation: A waiting period and a committee, that does sound official, friend. But Paul doesn't mention either one here. He says, "she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband."
That's right, baker. Paul says, "And a husband must not divorce his wife." So the wife has her command, and the husband has his. Neither one gets left out.
Not this time, friend. Right after talking about the wife, Paul says, "And a husband must not divorce his wife." So the husband has a command here too. It's not just aimed at her.

That's right, baker. Paul says, "If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her." Then he says the same for a woman with an unbelieving husband. This is the part he labels "I, not the Lord."

explanations.answer: Wait for them to believe first
explanations.explanation: That's not a condition Paul sets, friend. He says, "If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her." What matters in the verse is that the spouse is willing to live with the believer. Nothing says to wait for belief.

explanations.answer: Bring the matter to the elders
explanations.explanation: The elders don't show up in these verses, friend. Paul's instruction is short: if the unbelieving spouse is willing to live with the believer, the believer "must not divorce" them. He says this one is "I, not the Lord."

Yes, baker. Paul says, "Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy." He says it right after the part about the unbelieving spouse being sanctified through the believing one. Holy, not unclean, is his word for the children.
Not quite, friend. Paul says, "Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy." So the children are holy, and that's the reverse of what this statement says.

I know it sounds loyal, friend, but Paul says something different. He says, "But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go." He adds, "The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases." So there's no chasing involved.
That's right, baker. Paul says, "But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases." No chasing after them is required.

That's the word, baker. Paul says, "The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases." It comes right after he tells them to let the unbeliever go. And he follows it with, "God has called you to live in peace."
I see why it might fit, friend, but Paul never says anything about who is or isn't welcome. His words are, "The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases." Bound is the word he uses.
Trust is a big thing in any marriage, friend, but Paul doesn't use that word here. He says, "The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases." Bound is the one.

explanations.answer: How do you know whether you'll save your spouse
explanations.explanation: You've got it, baker. Paul asks, "How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?" He asks the wife and the husband the very same question. I think it's a question that makes you stop and think.

explanations.answer: Have you prayed for your spouse today
explanations.explanation: Praying for a spouse is a good habit, friend, but Paul doesn't ask that here. He asks, "How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband?" Then he turns it around and asks the husband about his wife.

explanations.answer: Will your spouse join you at church
explanations.explanation: Sitting together in the pew is a nice picture, friend, but that's not Paul's question. He asks, "How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?"

Close, friend, but Paul says it reaches further. He says each one should lead the life the Lord has assigned and God has called him to, and then adds, "This is what I prescribe in all the churches." All the churches, not just Corinth.
That's it, baker. Paul writes, "This is what I prescribe in all the churches." So it's not just for Corinth. It's the same instruction everywhere.
Right, baker. Paul asks, "Was a man already circumcised when he was called?" and answers, "He should not become uncircumcised." So he stays as he was when God called him.
An offering isn't in this verse, friend. Paul says, "Was a man already circumcised when he was called? He should not become uncircumcised." He's not asking for anything to be brought.
Paul doesn't ask anyone to confess anything here, friend. He says, "Was a man already circumcised when he was called? He should not become uncircumcised." The man just stays as he was.
Paul says the opposite, friend. He writes, "Was a man still uncircumcised when called? He should not be circumcised." So no, he stays as he was when God called him.
You've got it, baker. Paul says, "Was a man still uncircumcised when called? He should not be circumcised." It's the same instruction for both men. Each stays as he was when God called him.
Yes, baker. Paul says, "Keeping God's commandments is what counts." Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing, and he points to commandments as the thing that matters. Clear as day.
Feasts do sound like more fun, friend, but that's not Paul's word. He says, "Keeping God's commandments is what counts." Commandments is the one.
Traditions can feel very important, friend, but Paul doesn't use that word here. After saying circumcision and uncircumcision are nothing, he says, "Keeping God's commandments is what counts."

explanations.answer: Don't let it concern you but take freedom if you can
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Paul says, "Were you a slave when you were called? Do not let it concern you—but if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity." So he gives both parts. Don't be weighed down by it, and if freedom is possible, take it.

explanations.answer: Run away from your master as soon as you can
explanations.explanation: That's not what Paul says, friend. His words are, "Do not let it concern you—but if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity." He speaks of gaining freedom when it's possible. Running away isn't part of the verse.

explanations.answer: Stay a slave even if you're offered your freedom
explanations.explanation: Paul says the reverse, friend. He writes, "Do not let it concern you—but if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity." So when freedom is possible, he says to take it.

Yes, baker. Paul says, "he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord's freedman." A freedman is someone who has been set free. So the one called as a slave belongs to the Lord, and as a freedman.
A guest gets a nice seat, friend, but that's not Paul's word. He says, "he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord's freedman." Freedman is the word.

Heir is a big word, friend, and a good one, but Paul doesn't use it here. He writes, "he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord's freedman." A freedman is someone who's been set free.
You've got it, baker. Paul says, "Conversely, he who was a free man when he was called is Christ's slave." It's the flip side of the line about the slave. Both belong to the Lord.

Not this time, friend. Paul says, "Conversely, he who was a free man when he was called is Christ's slave." It's the flip side of what he just said about the slave who is the Lord's freedman. So the statement is true.
